paras: The lynching of three Black people in York County, South Carolina, is known from a single passing reference in a December 1888 dispatch, which recalled that a grand jury had been asked to look into "the lynching of three negroes in that county." The dispatch cited the case because the presiding judge, Judge Pressley, had told the grand jury that investigation was almost useless, as no jury would be likely to convict.

The coverage gives no date, town, names of the victims, accusation or description of the lynching itself. The only timing offered is that the judge's charge to the York grand jury came "some months" before mid-December 1888, so the lynching took place earlier still.

According to the correspondent, Judge Pressley told the grand jury that even if a bill were found against the lynchers, "it could hardly be expected that the jury would convict them." No report of an indictment, arrest or trial was found, and the same writer asserted that in South Carolina "no lyncher has ever been punished."

The reference appeared in a Charleston special to the New York Herald, reprinted by the Memphis Appeal on December 16, 1888, under the heading "South Carolina Opinion." The dispatch was written in response to the Birmingham sheriff's shooting of a mob and reported that Charleston lawyers and judges gave him "unstinted praise." Within that frame the York case served as evidence of impunity: the correspondent wrote that there had been "lynchings in abundance" in the state and called the judge's view "an extreme view, perhaps," while affirming its premise.

The same dispatch quoted F. W. Dawson of the Charleston News and Courier tracing lynching to "the lynching of colored men by whites for assaults upon white women," though he did not mention York. No contemporary report of the lynching, and no Black-press account, was found in the coverage.

bases: The only report calls it 'the lynching of three negroes' in York County, the subject of a grand jury inquiry (A2).

A2 names the case a lynching of three Black victims that a grand jury was asked to investigate as a crime, so an illegal killing is implied; the size of the group and any accusation or stated motive are not reported.
The case survives only as a one-sentence retrospective mention in a Charleston correspondent's dispatch reprinted in Memphis (A2); no report of the lynching itself was found.
